author: reek
body: TrackerApp, DiffusionApp and CallPage each build a command palette and none of them renders, filters or drives it: all three constants are mentioned exactly twice, at their signature and their definition. So the whole chapter is latent, which is the condition under which a wrong answer survives indefinitely and greets its first caller.

author: reek
body: The filter is asked with a query that matches nothing, because an empty result is where a highlight can leave the range its own list has.

author: reek
body: Fourteen commands, two past the twelve the palette will draw. Two of them carry a capital in the label, which is what the case question needs.

author: reek
body: A palette a person types into is asked to match what they typed, and the obvious query for the two commands whose labels begin with a capital is the lowercase one. Both cases are printed rather than one.

author: reek
body: The palette wraps deliberately at both ends, which is what a list a person arrows through should do.

author: reek
body: Navigating an EMPTY result is the case that decides whether the highlight can leave the list it indexes. Both directions are asked.

author: reek
body: Confirming with a highlight the visible list does not have must answer nothing rather than reading past either end of it.

author: reek
body: Now that navigating clamps, nothing reachable through the public calls leaves the highlight below zero, so the lower bound in the selection functions can no longer be reached that way. It is asked directly instead, by writing the field: a caller that builds or restores a state is not obliged to have arrived at it through the arrow keys, and a guard that only its own neighbour can fire is a guard nobody has tested.

author: reek
body: This line fires the bound in `palette-selected-command`, which without it answers `Just` a command whose every field is empty. It does NOT fire the one in `palette-confirm`: that read is equally out of range, but the action it comes back with is zero, which is what refusing answers too, so nothing printable here can tell them apart. The chapter says the same.

author: reek
body: Two rows of chrome and then one row per command, capped at twelve.

author: reek
body: A highlight past the twelve rows the palette draws is the question the cap raises: the selected command is real and off the bottom of what is rendered, so nothing on screen is marked.

author: reek
body: The window does not move until the selection would leave it, so the first screenful is still the first twelve commands.

author: reek
body: Each probe opens its own palette. These functions hand back the state they were given with a field written through, so driving one state three times measures a sequence and not three independent answers -- the second reading would start wherever the first left it.
